proof_text:
Let $(a_n)$ converge to $L$, and let $b_k = a_{n_k}$ be a subsequence,
where $n : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ is strictly increasing:
$n_1 < n_2 < n_3 < \cdots$. By induction on $k$, $n_k \geq k$ for all
$k \in \mathbb{N}$.

Let $\epsilon > 0$. Since $a_n \to L$, there exists $N \in \mathbb{N}$
such that for all $n \geq N$: $$ |a_n - L| < \epsilon. $$ Then for any
$k \geq N$, the index satisfies $n_k \geq k \geq N$, which guarantees:
$$ |b_k - L| = |a_{n_k} - L| < \epsilon. $$ Therefore, the subsequence
$(b_k)$ converges to the identical limit $L$.

Theorem:
given:
. S ::= a(n_) is \real.sequence
. T ::= b(k_) is \subsequence:of{S}
. L is \real
where: \converges.to{L}:for{S}
then: \converges.to{L}:for{T}
Documented:
. called: "Convergence is Inherited by Subsequences"
. description: "Every subsequence of a convergent sequence converges to the same
                limit. The converse fails without control of all indices."
